name: Pinhole surgical technique (gum recession)

lead: The pinhole surgical technique treats receding gums through a small opening in the gum instead of taking a graft from the palate. The payoff is covered roots and a more even gumline without a second surgical site.

Specialised instruments passed through the pinhole loosen the gum tissue so it can be moved over the exposed root, with or without added biomaterials. It was described in a 2012 retrospective study of 43 patients with 121 recession sites, and later case series and randomised trials have tested it alone and with platelet-rich fibrin or collagen membranes. The published studies are small.

paras: A trained dentist or periodontist performs it in the chair. It is chosen by people who want to avoid a palate donor site, and results are maintained with gentle brushing and regular checkups.

Complication rates are not detailed in the studies available, which are small case series and trials with limited long-term follow-up. Soreness and sensitivity are expected after gum procedures, and not every recession case is suited to this approach.

chain: Gum tissue loosened through small hole
Receded gums covered without a graft
angle.text: The pinhole technique moves existing gum back over exposed roots through a small opening, giving a more even gumline without taking tissue from the palate. The coverage is visible after healing; studies so far are small, with limited long-term follow-up.

lead: The pinhole surgical technique (PST), sometimes called the Chao pinhole technique, is a minimally invasive procedure for receding gums. A periodontist makes a single small entry hole in the gum above the recession, loosens the gum tissue through it with thin instruments and slides it coronally over the exposed root, so no tissue is harvested from the palate and often no stitches are needed.[1] For people who dislike long-looking teeth, exposed yellowish roots or uneven gum lines, it is a way to bring the gum margin back toward the crown and restore a more even, youthful smile line.

The technique was described in a 2012 retrospective study of 43 consecutive patients with 121 recession sites, presented as an alternative to free connective tissue grafts, which are regarded as the most predictable root-coverage method but leave a second surgical wound.[1] Since then case series, split-mouth trials and registered trials have tested PST alone and with platelet-rich fibrin (PRF) or collagen membranes, usually in small samples.[2][3][4][5][6][7]

In looksmaxxing circles gum recession comes up as part of facial and dental aesthetics, for example in a looksmax.org thread where an orthodontist's advice about gum recession, bite problems and jaw position is discussed.[8] Gum recession has many causes, so how much PST helps depends on the case and on treating the underlying cause.

paras: Free connective tissue grafts and coronally advanced flaps are the established way to cover exposed roots, and surgeons commonly describe the palatal donor site as a source of pain and bleeding.[1] PST was proposed to avoid that: one 2 to 3 mm entry incision is made, no releasing incisions, sharp dissection or sutures were required in the original series when a bioresorbable membrane was used, and the loosened gum is repositioned with collagen strips or a membrane placed to hold it.[1]

Indian case series describe PST as part of a minimal-invasion concept in periodontal plastic surgery, in which preserving existing tissue is favoured over replacing it, with an emphasis on 'pink esthetics'.[2][5] Case reports have added propolis[9] and PRF-based materials, and a cone-beam CT study assessed bone changes after minimally invasive periodontal surgery.[10]

sections.h: Gum recession and why people treat it
paras: Wikipedia lists periodontal disease as the most common cause of gum recession, along with hereditary thin gum tissue, tobacco use, trauma such as picking at the gum, tooth crowding or malposition, piercings and, in some reviews, vigorous tooth brushing, for which one review found the evidence inconclusive.[11] Visible effects include teeth that look longer, exposed roots, colour change and larger-looking spaces between teeth.[11] Recessions are classified with systems such as Miller's, and Class I and II (without interdental bone or papilla loss) are the ones in which complete root coverage is realistic.[11][1]

Standard grafting is done by a periodontist, usually under local anaesthesia, using pedicle grafts, palatal connective tissue or acellular dermal matrix; healing takes roughly two to four weeks.[11] Literature reviews also cover how recession is caused and how it links to wider oral health.[12][13]

Reports describe a short appointment under local anaesthetic, with the entry hole made at or near the mucogingival junction, instruments passed under the gum to release it from the root, and the tissue moved coronally and held in place with collagen strips or a membrane (and, in some versions, small sutures or buttons).[1] The original series averaged about 22 minutes per procedure.[1] A registered trial tested PST with and without buttons in multiple recessions.[14] Individual surgical details are taught in periodontal training and are not described here.

In the 2012 series the mean initial recession was 3.4 mm and the mean follow-up 18 months. For Class I and II sites, complete root coverage occurred in 81.2 percent and the mean reduction in defect size was 94.0 percent; counting Class III sites too, the figures were 69.4 and 88.4 percent. Patients reported a mean aesthetic satisfaction of 95.1 percent, reached in about a week, and complications were described as minimal.[1] This was a retrospective study by the technique's originators, without a control group.

Later controlled studies report more modest numbers. A split-mouth trial of 36 patients compared coronally advanced flap with connective tissue graft against PST with collagen membrane over one year: recession reduced by about 1.98 and 1.97 mm, and root coverage averaged about 65 and 64 percent, with no significant difference between them; keratinised tissue width increased only on the graft side.[7] A trial of 165 multiple adjacent recessions found that adding advanced PRF to PST gave significantly better reductions in recession depth and keratinised gingiva than PST alone, with both groups improving at 6 and 12 months.[4] A smaller trial of 10 patients with 51 recessions reported mean coverage of about 60 percent with PRF and about 50 percent with PST alone at six months.[6]

The original series reported minimal postoperative complications.[1] In the A-PRF split-mouth trial, pain scores in the first three days were lower on PRF sides than on collagen-membrane sides, and the authors described outcomes of both materials as not wholly satisfactory.[3] Because most studies are small and follow patients for months to a year, long-term durability and rates of rare complications are less documented than for conventional grafts. Gum recession can recur if causes such as plaque-related disease, tobacco use or tooth position are unaddressed.[11][13]

Gum recession is mentioned alongside bite, jaw and orthodontic concerns in looksmaxxing forums; one looksmax.org thread discusses an orthodontist's recommendation to treat gum recession and bite problems together.[8] Interest in PST specifically tends to centre on avoiding palate harvesting and on the faster recovery described in the clinical literature.

The 2012 retrospective study (43 patients, 121 sites) reported 81.2 percent complete coverage in Class I and II sites.[1] A 2025 split-mouth trial of 36 patients found PST with collagen membrane comparable to flap plus connective tissue graft at one year.[7] A 2024 split-mouth trial of 18 patients compared PST with A-PRF against PST with collagen membrane at three months; neither group showed the full recession coverage the authors hoped for, but the A-PRF group had less early pain.[3] A randomised trial of 165 multiple adjacent recessions favoured PST plus A-PRF over PST alone[4] and a 10-patient trial reported similar direction with PRF.[6] Case series from India describe PST in 5 and further patients,[2][5] a case report used propolis,[9] and a CBCT study examined bone changes.[10] A 2024 meta-analysis of A-PRF in gingival recession in general is available.[12] Registered trials compare PST with connective tissue graft (n=43), with the tunnel technique (n=21), with PRF (n=20) and with and without buttons (n=80).[15][16][17][14]

lore.intro: PST appears in forum discussion mostly as part of broader dental and jaw-aesthetics threads rather than as a stand-alone topic.[8]
